title: Matthew 24:45–51
context: Jesus closes the chapter with the faithful and wise servant set over the household to feed others in season, versus the wicked servant who assumes delay, abuses peers, and joins drunkards. Blessing and promotion meet the found-doing servant; sudden return, dismembering judgment, and hypocrites’ weeping meet the wicked one—bridge into chapter 25’s readiness parables.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Matthew 24:45–51.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Who then is the faithful and wise servant - Which of you aspires after this character? Wise - Every moment retaining the clearest conviction, that all he now has is only intrusted to him as a steward: Faithful - Thinking, speaking, and acting continually, in a manner suitable to that conviction.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 24:45–51)

reformed.quote: Luke relates this discourse of Christ at a different place from Matthew; and we need not wonder at this, for in the twelfth chapter, where (as we have formerly explained) he collects out of various discourses a summary of doctrine, he inserts also this parable. Besides, he introduces a general preface that the disciples should wait for their master, with their loins girt, and carrying burning lamps in their hands.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 24:45–51)

verses.text: “Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom his lord has set over his household, to give them their food in due season?
verses.arminianNotes:
Faithful and wise service means feeding the household in season. Authority is stewardship for others’ good.

Grace enables timely care. Leaders and members alike are invited to choose faithfulness over self-serving delay.
verses.reformedNotes:
The master sets a servant over the household for timed feeding. Office is gift and assignment under Christ’s lordship.

God appoints stewards. Wisdom and faithfulness are measured by care for those He entrusted.

verses.text: Blessed is that servant whom his lord finds doing so when he comes.
verses.arminianNotes:
Blessing rests on being so doing at the coming—caught in the act of faithful care.

Classical Arminians love this beatitude’s practicality: readiness looks like ongoing obedience. Grace sustains the doing until He appears.
verses.reformedNotes:
Beatitude for the servant found at the assigned work. The master’s coming evaluates present faithfulness.

God blesses what He commanded. Being found doing is evidence of a heart kept by the Master who returns.

verses.text: Most certainly I tell you that he will set him over all that he has.
verses.arminianNotes:
Promotion: set over all possessions. Faithful small trust leads to larger trust.

The Master rewards free fidelity. Grace that enabled service also delights to honor it without turning reward into wages that buy salvation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Solemn expansion of stewardship under the returning master. Greater charge follows proven care.

Christ’s “Most certainly” secures the servant’s future role. Reward is gracious appointment within the Master’s estate.

verses.text: But if that evil servant should say in his heart, ‘My lord is delaying his coming,’
verses.arminianNotes:
Wickedness begins in the heart’s speech: “My lord is delaying his coming.” Assumed delay licenses sin.

Arminians warn against delay-theology as moral solvent. Grace calls for living as if He may come soon—because presumption hardens.
verses.reformedNotes:
Internal monologue of delay births wickedness. The problem is theology before behavior.

False eschatology serves the flesh. God records the heart’s sentence that treats the master’s timing as slack.

verses.text: and begins to beat his fellow servants, and eat and drink with the drunkards,
verses.arminianNotes:
Abuse of peers plus drunken company—power turned cruel, holiness traded for party.

Delay-thinking harms people. Grace still invites the abuser to repent before the Master’s door; stop beating, leave the drunkards’ table.
verses.reformedNotes:
Violence toward fellow servants and fellowship with drunkards enact the delay-lie.

Misuse of household authority is judged as rebellion against the master. God sees both the blows and the cups.

verses.text: the lord of that servant will come in a day when he doesn’t expect it and in an hour when he doesn’t know it,
verses.arminianNotes:
Unexpected day and unknown hour fall on the wicked servant precisely because he gambled on delay.

The surprise is just. Grace offered time; presumption spent it. Come to readiness while the hour is still unrevealed.
verses.reformedNotes:
The master returns off the wicked servant’s clock. Hidden timing becomes judgment for the presumptuous.

God’s hour overrides human delay-talk. The coming is not late; the servant is wrong.

verses.text: and will cut him in pieces and appoint his portion with the hypocrites. That is where the weeping and grinding of teeth will be.
verses.arminianNotes:
Dismembering judgment and hypocrites’ place—weeping and gnashing. Empty religion ends in outer anguish.

Classical Arminians refuse to soften the close: this is a serious warning meant to turn hearers. Grace still pleads before that place; choose faithful feeding over hypocritical delay.
verses.reformedNotes:
Severe final verdict: cut in pieces, assigned with hypocrites, weeping and gnashing.

Jesus’ justice is not theatrical. God separates false stewards to the hypocrites’ doom; the warning guards the church and magnifies the blessedness of the faithful servant.
verses.keyContrast: Both take the wicked servant’s end as grave judgment. Arminians typically emphasize a sincere warning that summons repentance and faithful care now; Reformed interpreters stress the Master’s certain, unexpected justice that assigns hypocrites to weeping.
